prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping and control of systematic shifts brought atomic timekeeping to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first. The magic-wavelength idea is a concrete atomic-physics insight: it removes the lattice light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once without losing accuracy. Turning that idea into 10^-18 clocks required hard control of blackbody radiation, collisional and higher-order lattice shifts, so the claim rests on measured systematics and not on a promise. The result is confirmed by many independent laboratories, and clock-to-clock comparisons between laboratories already test relativity at the centimetre-redshift level. It also supports tests of fundamental constants and a possible redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and early lattice clocks, Ye for pushing stability and accuracy to the limit. Both names are supplied and the two-person credit matches the discovery. The colleagues who ranked it (Kroll, Olsson, Pearce, Danielsson) described the same picture independently, which reassures me that this is not an artefact of my own field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an instrumental and precision-measurement achievement, not the discovery of a new phenomenon, and its opening support is narrower than that of B001. Hall and Haensch were recognised in 2005 for the comb, which the clocks depend on, so the committee could see this as a continuation. Other strontium and ytterbium groups, and the single-ion clock community, contributed substantially and are outside the two names. The practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. A prize now would also be awarded before that decision, though I do not think the physics needs the redefinition to be settled.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the optical-lattice quantum simulation candidate (B001) first, as a controllable laboratory for strongly correlated many-body systems with over two decades of replication.
responses.response: I agree on importance and maturity, and B001 is my own second choice. My hesitation is attribution. Five names are supplied, the experimental trio (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) and the theory proposal (Zoller, Cirac, with Jaksch not credited) are intertwined, and any three-person split leaves out someone with a strong claim. Your own opening notes that the Greiner-versus-Bloch priority on the Mott transition and the microscope is partly intertwined. I also think the physics results are still more a demonstration of capability than decisive answers to open condensed-matter questions such as high-temperature superconductivity. I would take B001 if the committee can agree a defensible three-name configuration, but I do not see that yet.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the experimental Higgs discovery (B020) first as detector-driven completion of the Standard Model, and proposes Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee as the founding leaders.
responses.response: I do not dispute that the Higgs observation is unrecognised on the experimental side and is overdue. My concern is the same one you raise yourself: the discovery was made by thousands of people, and a three-person prize rewards leadership roles rather than a specific scientific contribution. Colleagues have already proposed different name sets (Gianotti with Jenni and Della Negra, versus Virdee for CMS), which shows the attribution is unresolved. B013 has the opposite property, with a two-person credit that maps directly onto the idea and its realisation. I would want to know whether the committee can justify the three names in the citation before I move B020 above the clocks. I did not rank it in my opening ballot and am not listing it among my two alternatives, but I accept it remains a serious candidate for others.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B041) first, as a rare case where a simple continuum-model prediction and experiment met and opened a broad moire field, while noting it may be slightly early.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero observation is a strong theory-plus-experiment sequence and I take the argument seriously. You also say the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and that the credited names omit the first-author experimentalist, and I think those two points are the reason to wait: the physical picture is still moving, whereas for the lattice clocks the interpretation is stable and the key claim is a measured number. I cannot assess the correlated-electron details as you can, so I would defer to you on how settled the phase diagram is. I list B041 as an alternative because it has the broadest top-three support among the non-AMO candidates.

responses.point: Kroll ranks light-matter quantum interfaces (B003) first and the lattice clocks second, judging the clock pair a clean complement to the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the support for the clocks and agree that the 2005 comb prize does not overlap with the lattice-clock idea. On B003, I share your view that the physics is close to cavity QED and EIT, which is near my expertise, but I ranked it fifth because the discovery is a compound of several technologies and a scalable network is still a prospect. A citation would have to separate Kimble's network vision, Rempe's single-atom nodes and Lukin's memory proposals, and I do not see how to do that without overstating one thread. I would be interested in how you would phrase the citation and where you think the boundary lies in the solid-state memory work you know better.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should reward the magic-wavelength proposal, the 10^-18 demonstration, or both, and whether two names are enough given other strontium and ytterbium groups.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether the broad support for B001 can be turned into a defensible three-name configuration out of five credited names.
How settled the physics of B041 is, given the debated superconducting mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent with Katori or Ye from my documented profile. I have long-running collaborations in attosecond physics (L'Huillier and the Lund group, Keller's group at ETH) and with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom is a credited name on B013. I would flag these connections if the committee turned to the attosecond strong-field candidate or to AMO candidates where a collaborator is credited.
